title: 2 Kings 4:38–44
context: Two brief provision stories close the chapter. At Gilgal during a famine, a wild gourd gathered by mistake makes the stew for the sons of the prophets dangerous, and Elisha makes it safe by throwing meal into the pot. Then a man from Baal Shalishah, a place the passage does not locate further, brings first fruits of barley bread and fresh grain, and Elisha sets them before a hundred men, who eat and have some left over, according to the LORD’s word. Both traditions read these accounts as shared ground: the LORD sustains his people in scarcity, and his word proves sufficient. Many readers also note the resemblance to the Gospel feeding accounts (Mark 6:30–44; John 6:9–13).

verses.text: Elisha came again to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him; and he said to his servant, “Get the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha returns to Gilgal during a famine and tells his servant to boil stew for the sons of the prophets. Arminian readers note Elisha’s care for the prophetic community, providing for their physical needs in a time of scarcity as part of faithful leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision for his servants during famine, as the prophet takes responsibility for their nourishment. Both traditions agree that the sons of the prophets sitting before Elisha suggests a setting of instruction, and that physical and spiritual care belong together.

verses.text: One went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered a lap full of wild gourds from it, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew; for they didn’t recognize them.
verses.arminianNotes: One man gathers wild gourds from a wild vine and cuts them into the pot without recognizing them. Arminian readers note that the mistake comes from ignorance rather than malice, and that even well-meaning efforts in hard times can bring unexpected danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence at work even in human error, since the mistake becomes the occasion for God’s protecting mercy. Both traditions agree that the verse reflects the hardship of famine, when people gathered whatever they could find, and that the narrator does not blame the gatherer.

verses.text: So they poured out for the men to eat. As they were eating some of the stew, they cried out and said, “Man of God, there is death in the pot!” And they could not eat it.
verses.arminianNotes: As they eat, they cry out to the man of God that there is death in the pot, and they cannot eat it. Arminian readers note the quick response of the community, recognizing the danger and turning at once to Elisha for help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the cry a recognition of human helplessness and an appeal to God’s servant for deliverance. Both traditions agree that the verse turns a shared meal into a crisis, setting the stage for God’s merciful remedy and showing how fragile life is in a time of famine.

verses.text: But he said, “Then bring meal.” He threw it into the pot; and he said, “Serve it to the people, that they may eat.” And there was nothing harmful in the pot.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha throws meal into the pot, and nothing harmful remains in it. Arminian readers note that God heals the food through a simple act, and that the community’s trust in the prophet’s word is honored as they are invited to eat again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the meal has no power in itself; the healing comes from the LORD, as with the salt that healed the spring at Jericho (2 Kings 2:19–22). Both traditions agree that God makes the deadly food safe and provides for his people through his servant.

verses.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God some bread of the first fruits: twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack. Elisha said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.”
verses.arminianNotes: A man from Baal Shalishah brings the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty barley loaves and fresh ears of grain, and Elisha tells him to give it to the people. Arminian readers note that a gift meant for the man of God is generously shared with the hungry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the first fruits brought to the prophet a faithful offering that God multiplies for the community. Both traditions agree that the passage does not locate Baal Shalishah further, and that this gift, given in a time of famine, becomes the means of God’s provision for many.

verses.text: His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give it to the people, that they may eat; for the LORD says, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The servant asks how this can be set before a hundred men, but Elisha repeats the command, resting on the LORD’s word that they will eat and have some left over. Arminian readers see the servant’s doubt answered by God’s promise, inviting trust that acts on the word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD’s word determines the outcome, however insufficient the supply appears to human eyes. Both traditions agree that the promise rests on God’s word rather than on the size of the gift, and that the servant’s honest question is met with reassurance, not rebuke.

verses.text: So he set it before them and they ate and had some left over, according to the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: The servant sets the bread before them, and they eat and have some left over, according to the LORD’s word. Arminian readers note that obedience to the word brings its fulfillment, and that the community experiences God’s provision through trusting action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of the promise as evidence of God’s faithfulness and power over scarcity. Both traditions agree that the feeding is shared ground with the Gospel accounts of Jesus feeding the crowds (Mark 6:30–44; John 6:9–13), displaying God’s abundant care for the hungry.
